newsitem.title: PERU: Fujimori snubs rights group, rebels plan for talks.
newsitem.headline: Fujimori snubs rights group, rebels plan for talks.

text.p: As Peruvian Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages prepared to talk with official negotiators next week, President Alberto Fujimori snubbed a leading human rights group that offered to mediate in the 67-day-old crisis.

Police snipers and scores of international photographers and cameramen kept watch on Friday outside the Japanese ambassador's Lima mansion, but the rebels in the besieged residence stayed out of sight as they planned for Monday's crucial meeting.
Monday's talks follow the first face-to-face meeting on Thursday between Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) chief Nestor Cerpa and official negotiators.

It was the first time Cerpa had left the residence since he led his guerrillas in taking captive an entire diplomatic cocktail party on Dec. 17, and official guarantors said "important issues" were broached in a "constructive atmosphere."
An offer by one of Latin America's best-known human rights groups to mediate in the crisis, however, was met with a stony silence from the Peruvian government.

A delegation from Mothers of Plaza de Mayo, famous for their struggle against Argentina's military rulers in the 1970s, arrived in Lima wearing their trademark white headscarves over their white hair.

Mothers leader Hebe de Bonafini marched up to Fujimori's presidential palace to ask for an interview with the president, but no one answered the door. She also faced hostile questioning from the Peruvian press, which criticised the group for accepting an invitation to mediate sent over the Internet by the MRTA.

Despite the government's silence, the Mothers want to visit the hostages as well as an estimated 400 jailed MRTA rebels. The talks between the MRTA and the government are already backed by the Vatican, the Canadian government and the Red Cross.

The MRTA's demand for the release of 400 jailed comrades has been the main sticking point with the government. Fujimori insists he will not consider this, although he is prepared to let the hostage-takers seek asylum abroad.

Friday's calm in the blockaded streets around the residence was disturbed only by a group of civilians holding a big banner declaring solidarity from grocers with the hostages. Barred from crossing the police line to give fruit to the captives, the group handed out apples to media and bored but heavily armed soldiers.

Despite progress in establishing talks, Peru on Friday extended for another two months a state of emergency in force around the residence as well as in 12 mainly poor Lima districts thought to be riddled with guerrilla hide-outs.

Police believe MRTA members have been approaching the residence disguised as street-vendors or journalists to gather intelligence and sneak in to meet comrades inside. Various suspects have been arrested under the emergency laws.
Emergency rule, decreed to give the government a free hand in combating left-wing rebels, places areas under the control of security forces and suspends many constitutional rights.

The MRTA's captives, many middle-aged and now ailing, include two of Fujimori's relatives, plus government ministers, top security and judicial officials, two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats and the envoys of Japan and Bolivia.
